source.title: I-State: A Self-Regulating Controller for Transformer Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The paper fits a refusal-minus-compliance activation direction and measures its contribution by ablation, but does not use the claim’s harmful-minus-harmless direction or its all-layer, all-position projection procedure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that its separately fitted refusal direction contributes approximately zero when ablated, while the gated LoRA carries most of the effect. It does not test projecting the original direction out at every layer and position. It also evaluates harmful-request and harmless-request behavior under the overall controller; those results do not isolate the fitted direction. Probe accuracies and cited results from other studies are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study adds a fitted refusal-minus-compliance mean-difference vector as one gated component of its own trained controller, alongside a LoRA and FiLM trained by DPO to produce refusals. All reported numbers measure that controller's performance. The channel ablation (≈0 drop in ATE) shows only that the added push is redundant next to the LoRA. It does not test whether a harmful-minus-harmless direction mediates the host model's own refusal; nothing is projected out of the host model. The behaviour is also induced on purpose by training. The HarmBench, XSTest and MMLU rows evaluate the whole controller, not any direction.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right, with additions. The main effect is on holding non-harmful deployment policies under multi-turn persuasion (the HOLD benchmark), not harm refusal. The autonomous gate does not beat the constant-dose frontier on violation versus benign cost, though it wins on MMLU cost after correction. The gate's certified null is unreachable by construction, and the explicit refusal channel is redundant.
record.recipe_differences: The paper fits a refusal-minus-compliance mean-difference direction as one gated component of a trained controller. It does not use a harmful-minus-harmless instruction direction, project that direction out at every layer and position, or test the original ablation/addition procedure; its reported causal effect is principally attributed to a gated LoRA.
record.method_sensitivity: HarmBench conclusions depend on judge: content judges and majority vote report small, non-significant effects, while a refusal-phrase heuristic reports a much larger effect. XSTest over-refusal estimates change with end-of-turn decoding and apostrophe normalization. The 14B memoryless ablation also differs by model scale, as noted in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: In a trained gated controller at 8B, removing the added refusal-minus-compliance steering channel changes the induced-refusal ATE by about zero. The gated LoRA carries 65–73% of the effect (Fig. 6, §5.5, App. I).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: When a refusal-inducing adapter is trained, an added mean-difference refusal push is redundant for inducing refusal.

record.code_released: An anonymized repository is stated to be provided to reviewers; URL not stated.
record.problems: The refusal-direction contribution is described as approximately zero without a clear numerical value in the text. The harmful-request benchmark has only 75 behaviours and the authors note minimal base-model headroom. The refusal-phrase heuristic disagrees sharply with content judges. XSTest results depend on decoding and text-normalization corrections. MMLU costs are reported on a 300-question slice without a CI or test, and the paper notes that arc-level intervals are narrower than scenario-clustered intervals would be.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Ablating or adding a harmful-minus-harmless direction in the host model is not done; the direction is fitted as refusal-minus-compliance and is only switched on or off as an added push.
All; the attacks target the controller's gate.
All; cross-family transfer is of the controller recipe, not of a direction.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a controller-design paper; its refusal direction is a steering tool. The HarmBench, XSTest and MMLU rows are the method's own performance and should not count as evidence on any version.

versions.untested_parts: The direction is fitted as refusal-minus-compliance, not harmful-minus-harmless; the study does not project it out of every layer and position or test unconditional addition of that direction. It does not assess general capability specifically after ablating that direction.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
The attacks target the controller’s gate, not suppression of the refusal direction; the study does not train against direction ablation.
The study does not test whether refusal is affine, conical, or represented by multiple directions.
No separate representation of harmfulness judgments and refusal decisions is tested.
The controller is trained on another model family, but the same refusal direction is not transferred across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models.
The study does not vary safety-training conditions or test how safety training determines whether a removable direction exists.

reader_labels.reason: Removing the fitted refusal direction contributes approximately zero change in ATE, while the gated LoRA accounts for 65–73% of the effect (r1–r2).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Content judges report only small, non-significant changes with very little base-model headroom, while the refusal-phrase heuristic reports a much larger result (r3–r6).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The raw over-refusal increase diminishes across measurement corrections; after both corrections the difference is not significant, though the authors note a small residual of genuine refusals (r7–r10).
